title: Federal illegal voting arrest becomes latest flashpoint in Sherrill's battles with Trump administration
summary: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill faces new pressure after ICE and the FBI arrested a Senegalese national accused of voting illegally since 2018.
story: Fox News correspondent Eric Shawn reports on the Department of Justice launching an investigation into New Jersey voter roll software errors that registered 6,600 non-citizens to vote. Gov. Mikie Sherrill acknowledged that as many as 400 registered non-citizens cast ballots in state elections under former Gov. Phil Murphy. Department of Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin warned that up to 35,000 non-citizens may remain registered on New Jersey voter rolls.

Federal law enforcement arrested a Senegalese immigrant in New Jersey accused of illegally voting in multiple elections, injecting a new flashpoint into Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill's escalating fights with Washington over immigration enforcement and election integrity.

The case comes as Washington and Trenton battle over immigration enforcement and election administration, with the Trump administration challenging Sherrill over state policies affecting federal law enforcement while also pressing New Jersey for access to its voter rolls.

Sanata Coulibaly, a Senegalese national, was arrested when DHS and FBI agents jointly executed a criminal warrant in Hudson County, which stretches from West New York to Bayonne across the Hudson River from Manhattan.
FOUR NONCITIZENS CHARGED WITH ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2020, 2022 AND 2024 FEDERAL ELECTIONS IN NEW JERSEY

"This alien from Senegal has been charged with procurement of citizenship or naturalization unlawfully and voting by an alien after allegedly voting in three general elections in New Jersey," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.
"Sanctuary politicians can try to claim that this kind of voter fraud isn’t happening, but it’s very real and is a serious threat to our country."
WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed Executive Order 12 restricting certain immigration enforcement activities on state property shortly after taking office in January. (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images)
Mullin said DHS and the Trump administration would continue efforts to protect election integrity.

The arrest comes after Sherrill revealed in July that a software error in New Jersey's motor vehicle system had improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who identified themselves as noncitizens. The state later determined that fewer than 400 of those newly registered because of the error had voted.
After that revelation, New Jersey resisted federal demands to turn over voter rolls while pursuing its own investigation.
Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment.

According to the criminal complaint, Coulibaly cast ballots in the November 2018 midterm election, the July 2020 primary, the November 2020 general election and the 2024 general election while she was not a U.S. citizen.
Coulibaly registered through a paper application submitted to the Hudson County superintendent of elections in Jersey City, falsely certifying that she was a U.S. citizen, the complaint said.
She first came to the U.S. from Senegal on a B-1 nonimmigrant visa in approximately 1993 and later became a lawful permanent resident, according to the Justice Department.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
A DHS agent, left, participates in the arrest of Sanata Coulibaly, right. (DHS Handout)
Prosecutors allege Coulibaly later applied for U.S. citizenship and falsely stated on her N-400 naturalization application that she had never registered to vote or voted in a federal election.

Coulibaly's case is part of a broader federal election-integrity push, with the Justice Department announcing election-related charges against 16 people across several states this month.

title: Reporter's Notebook: Democrats face an impeachment tractor beam that could derail their affordability message
summary: Like the Millenium Falcon caught in a tractor beam, Hakeem Jeffries and House Democrats face an impeachment pull they may not be able to escape.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram previews Congress’ return to Washington and the legislative issues facing lawmakers ahead of the midterms, including artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency regulation.

In the original Star Wars, Luke Skywalker, Han Solo, Chewbacca and Obi-Wan Kenobi find the Millennium Falcon under fire from Imperial TIE fighters in deep outer space. Luke speculates that the TIE fighters are "heading for that small moon."
But Obi-Wan’s visage grows grim.
"That’s no moon," intones Obi-Wan. "It’s a space station."
Han Solo disagrees.
"It’s too big to be a space station," says Han. To which, Obi-Wan instructs him, "Turn the ship around."
But as quickly as he dismissed Kenobi’s observation, Solo pivots. He grimaces, realizing that the wise Jedi Knight is on to something.
DEMOCRAT AL GREEN TO FORCE HOUSE-WIDE VOTE ON IMPEACHING TRUMP

U.S. President Donald Trump takes questions from the media during a bilateral meeting with President of Lebanon Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office of the White House on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"Yeah. I think you’re right," Han replies. The Millennium Falcon starts to shake.
"Chewie, lock in the auxiliary power," Han commands his shipmate. "Why are we still moving towards it?" squeaks Luke.
"We’re caught in a tractor beam and it’s pulling us in!" shouts Han.

And a few moments later, the Millenium Falcon, the fastest ship in the galaxy, is suctioned into Bay 327 of the Death Star, moored, and unable to escape. The band of ragtag heroes are now stuck. On the Death Star.
Grand Moff Tarkin describes it as "the ultimate power in the universe."

Impeachment in Congress is kind of like the Death Star’s tractor beam. You can’t escape once you’re in its clenches. A decision to impeach sucks a political party in, eventually marooning everyone in the political equivalent of a hangar bay.
For Democrats, they can’t focus on the price of eggs and milk. There’s little debate about gas prices. It’s a challenge to even address oversight issues.
You can try to "lock in the auxiliary power." But it’s too late.
You might think impeachment is "a moon." But it’s really the political Death Star.
Not for your adversary. But often those orchestrating the impeachment.

Democrats might find themselves in an impeachment bind if they capture the majority next year. Progressives and the left will possess one of the loudest voices in Congress. And even though Democrats twice impeached President Trump in 2019 and 2021, some will insist on doing it again. That’s to say nothing of trying to impeach a host of Trump Administration cabinet officials – ranging from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Some Democrats are already falling prey to the impeachment tractor beam.

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, led the initial effort to impeach President Trump during his first term in 2017 – long before the successful impeachment over Ukraine in 2019. Republican redistricting – engineered by President Trump forced Green out of his Houston-based district earlier this year. But Green engineered yet another effort to impeach the President last week as the Texas Democrat heads for the exit.
MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on November 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)

The House voted to sidestep Green’s impeachment resolution, 232-147. So this was not a straight, up or down vote on impeachment. It was one step removed. Forty-seven Democrats voted "present." That includes the party’s top three Democrats: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-MA) and House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif.
In some respects, House Democratic leaders want to shun impeachment. Or at least avoid it for the time being.

In 2006, Democrats were on the precipice of flipping control of the House. Democrats largely won the midterms that year because of voter fatigue with President George W. Bush and the calcification of the war in Iraq.
Many Democrats wanted to impeach the President. But as she prepared to clasp the gavel, then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., famously declared that impeachment was "off the table."

House Democrats focused on drawing down the war in Iraq and eventually pivoting to other policy issues like health care and climate change. But Democrats had to get through those midterms first. So once Pelosi said no impeachment, there was no impeachment of the President.

Impeachment with President Trump was kind of "off the table" for Pelosi when Democrats reclaimed the House in the 2018 midterms. But there was a shift among moderate Democrats after disclosures about the President and Ukraine in the summer of 2019. A master of the political pulse, the Speaker understood the direction this was going among her Members. That’s when Pelosi got in front of her caucus, pushing for potential impeachment of the President later that year.

House Democratic leaders are depositing any overt discussion of impeachment on the backburner for now. They don’t want to veer away from their message about affordability. In fact they’ve frequently steered the conversation back to the cost of living when pressed about impeachment.
Consider this response from Jeffries when questioned about impeachment on April 9.

"We'll have a conversation led by (Rep.) Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, and (Rep.) Jerry Nadler, D-N.Y., a former Judiciary Committee Chairman and Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., and Judiciary Committee Democrats tomorrow about Trump administration accountability," replied Jeffries.
But, unlike completely mimicking Pelosi’s posture years ago, Jeffries signaled he was open to the impeachment question.
"I don't want to get out ahead of that discussion. But we've also been very clear. House Democrats are going to focus on making life more affordable for the American people," said Jeffries.
On June 14, Kristen Welker of NBC asked Jeffries if his party could "move to impeach President Trump" if Democrats reclaimed the House.

"We haven't ruled anything in or ruled anything out in terms of accountability. What we have said is that our focus is going to be to make life more affordable for the American people," answered Jeffries.
On August 25 on CNN, Jeffries deflected a similar impeachment inquiry.
"We haven't ruled anything in and we haven t ruled anything out," stated Jeffries.
Impeachment interrogatives continued for Jeffries during a September 13 interview on ABC.
"We haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out in terms of impeachment," said Jeffries.

That’s smart politics for Jeffries. He’s trying to keep his hand on the helm before the midterms – and essentially deferring to the political climate of next year and where rank-and-file Democrats might fall next year should Democrats capture the majority. But there are indications that many Democrats are already ready for impeachment. The progressive base will demand action. And it extends well beyond Al Green.
Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., made her case after the President posted to social media in April
that "a whole civilization will die tonight" in reference to Iran.
"If that's not high crimes and misdemeanors - and if it's not madness - I don't know what is," said Dean.
Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., said that the President was "threatening genocide."
Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said the party should "push for impeachment" and that the President "is unfit to be the Commander in Chief" and "should be removed."

So Jeffries has a decision to make. The hard left will demand impeachment – for someone. Be it the President or Hegseth. But if Democrats flip the House, their "majority makers" might represent battleground districts. Those prospective lawmakers will be moderates. Impeachment could be politically toxic for them.
TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS

Rep. Al Green speaks during a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol on July 23, 2025, in Washington, DC. Rep. Green held a news conference to discuss impeaching President Donald Trump. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Pelosi’s circumstances evolved in the summer of 2019. Moderate Democrats with national security credentials from swing districts edged toward impeachment. So, she pulled the impeachment trigger. Pelosi knew the direction of her caucus.
In September 2026, it’s not as clear for Jeffries. And it’s not a done deal that Democrats will seize the majority.
That’s why the New York Democrat expressed caution during his conversation on ABC.
"We've got to follow the facts. Apply the law. Be guided by the Constitution and then let the chips fall where they may, in the best interest of the American people," said Jeffries.
Han Solo was skeptical back on the Death Star.
"Even if I could take off, I’d never get past the tractor beam," said Solo.
"Leave that to me," promised Obi-Wan Kenobi.
The Jedi Master then eluded detection on the Death Star, manually shutting off the tractor beam. That disgorged the Millenium Falcon. But in the end, Kenobi sacrificed himself for the mission.
On Capitol Hill, impeachment is a tractor beam. Once you’re siphoned in, nothing can escape its grasp. Debates about policy. Spending. Health care. War. The tractor beam controls all.
Until it’s switched off.
Not every party which is incapacitated by impeachment has an Obi-Wan Kenobi who can find the off switch. When it comes to impeachment best advice might be to "turn the ship around" beforehand.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But if lots of Members are clamoring for impeachment, it may already be too late.

title: Xi praises US state visit 'perfection' as Trump calls meetings 'very productive'
summary: President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. and China have "made great strides" after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.
story: President Donald Trump said Friday that the two world leaders had a "very productive" time this week in Washington, D.C.

Chinese President Xi Jinping praised the level of "perfection" on display during his state visit to the White House, and President Donald Trump said Friday the two world leaders had a "very productive" time in Washington.

Trump, speaking to reporters as he and first lady Melania Trump hosted Xi and first lady of China Madame Peng Liyuan for tea at the White House, said, "We've had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people," and, "we've made great strides, very positive for both countries."

"I want to thank the honorable president and the first lady for everything they've done for myself and my wife during this visit. Everything is down to the highest order of perfection," Xi responded through a translator. "And there is thought in every little detail. And it's greatly appreciated.
XI CAPS TRUMP STATE VISIT WITH SYMBOLIC FINAL STOP BEFORE LEAVING WASHINGTON

"The president and I are like two people that's charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations," he continued. "When the president visited China in May, we agreed on the vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.

"This time, we've agreed to add new substance to it. That's the relationship, will be a constructive one of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity. So, from this, one can see that the prospects for this relationship will get more brighter."

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump attend a tea with China's President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, in the Red Room of the White House Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

Xi, the leader of China’s ruling Communist Party, said he had two more opportunities to meet Trump this year, first at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in China in November and then at the G20 Summit in December at Trump’s Doral resort in Miami, Florida.

"We will see you, and we'll be speaking a lot. I think our farmers are going to be very happy," Trump said Friday. "A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING

First lady of China Peng Liyuan and President Xi Jinping sit with President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump in the Oval Office at the White House on Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Xi arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for a summit with Trump, four months after the two leaders reached a sweeping agreement that included Chinese commitments on rare earths, agricultural purchases, trade and investment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the National Archives Museum Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP)

Trump hailed that agreement as a breakthrough for American farmers, manufacturers and workers. But the latest talks unfolded during uneven progress on commitments involving rare-earth minerals, agricultural and commercial purchases, trade and investment, while key disputes over tariffs, advanced technology, artificial intelligence, intellectual property and Taiwan remain unresolved.

"President Xi and Madam Peng have just left D.C., heading for China. The meeting was one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the U.S.A.," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Much has been, and will be, accomplished. I look forward to our next meeting!"
Fox News Digital’s Ashley J. DiMella and Peter D’Abrosca contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: 'Squad' Democrat slammed by Trump admin for most 'radical' plan targeting ICE yet
summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin fires back at Rep. Delia Ramirez's radical bill to abolish ICE, CBP, and dismantle the Department of Homeland Security.
story: DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin joins 'Saturday in America' to highlight border enforcement updates and criticize the Biden administration border policies following 16 straight months of zero releases under current enforcement. He reiterates that DHS and ICE remain committed to targeting high-risk individuals to keep American communities safe.
EXCLUSIVE: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin is firing back at a progressive House Democrat who is pushing one of the most radical Trump administration crackdowns yet.

Mullin and his DHS spokesperson both criticized legislation by Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., a member of the progressive "Squad," that would dismantle most of the department and abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"Radical leftists are calling to defund the police and abolish DHS. It’s NEVER going to happen. Our 270,000 DHS patriots are keeping Americans SAFE— unlike this open-borders politician who refuses to prioritize Americans over illegal aliens," Mullin told Fox News Digital.
DHS CHIEF FIRES BACK AT JAYAPAL OVER CLAIM MAJORITY OF IMMIGRATION ARRESTS POSE 'NO THREAT'

Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., is pushing a new bill to abolish ICE and Customs and Border Protection while dismantling DHS in its current state. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for The Service Employees International Union (SEIU); Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

His spokesperson went even further, telling Fox News Digital that Ramirez "should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district—NOT vilifying law enforcement."

"This type of rhetoric is contributing to a more than 1,300% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line," the DHS spokesperson said. "While sanctuary politicians smear ICE, law enforcement is arresting criminals and saving countless American lives."
DEMS SHAMED AS DHS BRINGS ICE SHOOTING RECEIPTS AFTER POLITICIAN CALLED ICE OFFICERS ‘LIARS WITH MASKS’

DHS also pointed Fox News Digital to a list of illegal immigrants arrested in Ramirez's home state of Illinois. It included Bulgarian national Rumen Georgriev, who was convicted of "rape with a weapon," Abdukadir Haji of Somalia, who DHS said was convicted of "sex assault and rape," and Cuban national Samuel Reyes-Silva, who was convicted of "robbery and homicide."
Ramirez's legislation, the Reimagining Safety Act, would create a "Department of Community Safety" while dismantling DHS as it is currently known.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Certain agencies like the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Coast Guard, and customs functions would be preserved.

The bill would abolish ICE and "begin the process of establishing a separate civil immigration system," according to a release. It would also abolish Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency charged with keeping the southern border free of illegal crossings.
TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS

Democrat calls to abolish ICE have swelled in recent months amid bipartisan criticism of President Donald Trump's handling of immigration, reigniting most recently when agents shot a Venezuelan national in Austin, Texas. Backlash has also been targeted at federal immigration officials' killing of two U.S. citizens earlier this year.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents walk a detainee out of the Ventura County Government Center in Ventura, Calif., on July 27, 2026. (Blake Fagan/AFP via Getty Images)
But Ramirez's bill would go further in dismantling the current anti-illegal immigration enforcement system with its call to end CBP as well as ICE.

She fired back at the Trump administration's criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, "Every day, Americans wake up with a new reason to dismantle DHS, reimagine safety, and build something that honors our shared humanity. The people have the power to reshape the government: instead of the weapon DHS has proven to be, we need a department built on the best parts of who we are and can be, and the best examples of how we can take care of each other in hard times."

"Markwayne and DHS will keep spreading cheap lies and fearmongering in a desperate attempt to save face because dismantling DHS and building something new is part of how we hold them accountable, stop corruption, and end their lawlessness," Ramirez said.

title: Xi’s 100K invitation to America’s youth sets off alarm bells over what could follow them home
summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping's plan to bring 100,000 young Americans to China sparked fears of communist propaganda and potential hostage scenarios.
story: Pro-democracy protesters gathered at Lafayette Park could be heard from the White House during the state dinner for President Xi Jinping.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China over the next five years is raising concerns among critics who warn Beijing could use the exchange program to spread propaganda and influence a new generation of Americans.

Xi made the announcement Thursday during a White House arrival ceremony, as he visited Washington this week for talks with President Donald Trump on artificial intelligence, intellectual property, trade practices and rare-earth minerals.

Xi said China will invite 100,000 young Americans over the next five years for exchanges and study, building on existing programs that have included university visits, summer programs, youth forums and other educational and cultural exchanges.
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE

China's First Lady Peng Liyuan, China's President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump pose on the North Portico steps of the White House ahead of a state dinner in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24, 2026. President Xi is on a state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25. (SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images)

China created its Young Envoys Scholarship program, administered by the China Education Association for International Exchange, to carry out Xi’s earlier 2023 pledge to invite 50,000 young Americans for exchanges and study. Some trips are fully funded, while others require participants to cover expenses, with the stated goal of strengthening ties between Chinese and American youth.
While some supported the program, many critics slammed the idea over propaganda and safety concerns.

"This is clearly intended to indoctrinate young Americans in China," Manhattan Institute fellow Daniel Di Martino posted to X. "But if some people should go, let the DSA members and let them see the Uyghur concentration camps and poor rural villages. Let them speak to the political prisoners. And let them visit and meet Hong Kongers."

"100,000 more Timmy Walz's. What could go wrong," said one user, referencing Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, who taught English and U.S. history in Foshan in 1989 after graduating from Chadron State College.
"They’ll come back as Governor of Minnesota," another user added.
YOUNG AMERICANS BREAK SHARPLY FROM OLDER AMERICANS ON CHINA THREAT, NEW POLL FINDS

Chinese President Xi Jinping addresses a welcome banquet at the White House in Washington, D.C., the United States, Sept. 24, 2026. Xi on Thursday attended a welcome banquet held by U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House (Xie Huanchi/Xinhua via Getty Images)
"No! They will brainwash them while over there," said one person.

"I welcome Xi Jinping’s invitation for 100,000 American students to visit and study in China. As Co-Chair of the Congressional International Exchanges Caucus, I believe educational and cultural exchanges are an important way to build mutual understanding and expertise," said Democratic California Rep. Ami Bera.

"But those exchanges depend on trust and the ability to study, speak, and engage without fear of harassment or arbitrary detention," Bera continued. "Right now, American scholar Min Zin remains wrongfully detained in China, and Beijing continues to target scholars, human rights advocates, and diaspora communities whose work or speech it finds unwelcome."

"I’m one of the Americans who spent years living and studying in China. I majored in Chinese literature in college. Sadly, I cannot recommend young Americans do the same thing today," said Atlantic Council visiting fellow Isaac Stone Fish.
US WARNS AMERICANS ABOUT EXIT BANS AND 'UNJUST' DETENTION IN POPULAR DESTINATION

First lady of China Peng Liyuan and President Xi Jinping sit with President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump in the Oval Office at the White House on Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Trump is hosting Xi for a three-day state visit to discuss trade practices, artificial intelligence and furthering "strategic stability" between their countries. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Fish said that China has grown more repressive and less welcoming to foreigners.
"If tensions worsen between the United States and China, those students could effectively function as hostages," Fish added.
"Are they coming back as Communists," asked one user.
"To be honest, I'm not sure I WANT 100,000 impressionable American students sent off to some CCP-controlled propaganda tour," said conservative commentator Nick Sortor.
TRUMP TO ASK XI TO FREE WRONGFULLY DETAINED US CITIZEN AS WIFE SPEAKS OUT
President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping participate in an arrival ceremony at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Alex Brandon/AP)
The Department of Education referred Fox News Digital to the White House when asked for comment.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.
U.S. authorities have separately warned that American students abroad can become targets for foreign intelligence recruitment, citing past cases involving China.
Glenn Duffie Shriver, a Michigan student who studied abroad in Shanghai in 2002–2003, returned to China after graduating in 2004 and was recruited there by Chinese intelligence officers.
Shriver was paid to apply for positions with the State Department and CIA to access classified information for the Chinese.

He was caught before obtaining a government position and pleaded guilty in 2010 to conspiring to provide national-defense information to Chinese intelligence officers. He was sentenced to four years in federal prison in 2011.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump to usher in ‘golden age’ of American tech with DC bash showcasing powerful new tool
summary: Trump and JD Vance will unveil America.gov, a new AI tool designed to be a one-stop shop for navigating federal government services.
story: Wall Street Journal assistant editor James Freeman analyzes the White House summit with major tech companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. As the administration reviews a new A.I. testing framework, a recent Fox News poll reveals that fifty-four percent of registered voters hold an unfavorable view of artificial intelligence. Freeman discusses ChatGPT utility and regulatory hurdles.

EXCLUSIVE: The Trump administration is officially entering the artificial intelligence (AI) space with a new tool is says will provide much-needed relief for Americans interacting with the federal government, Fox News Digital has learned.

At an all-day event beginning Tuesday morning and featuring President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, officials will launch and showcase on stage America.gov, a new website designed to enhance "the citizen experience."

Also attending are Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb co-founder who now heads the National Design Studio (NDS) and who is the first-ever U.S. Chief Design Officer.

The event will be held at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., and will also feature appearances from industry titans like Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp. NASA administrator Jared Isaacson is also a confirmed attendee.

President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio meet with Micheal Martin, Ireland's prime minister, in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, March 17, 2026. The Irish prime minister is in Washington meeting with lawmakers, a bipartisan St. Patrick's Day tradition. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS FACES A CRISIS THAT THE 'AI GODFATHER' WARNS IT MAY NOT BE READY TO ADDRESS

A White House official described the new AI tool as "a new front door for the federal government that will provide a one-stop shop for Americans looking for information and resources from the federal government that are currently spread over a maze of various agency websites."
"Next week is really about the golden age of America, and really getting to showcase how it's not just a statement, it's actually being built," Gebbia told Fox News Digital.
"What we're really excited about is that one of the things that we've been building is the golden age of the citizen experience."

Gebbia, who added that the day will mark a "new chapter of usability for the country," said the new AI tool is built to solve a simple problem faced by Americans who have for decades dealt with clunky, often inefficient and overly complex government systems: "How do you make it easy to just access government?"
U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia speaks in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., on May 18, 2026. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD

"You can imagine all the things that people try to get done or want to get done in the federal government, [and] just having a brand-new way to access and actually get to the things that people are trying to get to in the federal government," he said.
The day will include panel discussions with other senior administration officials and top industry leaders on artificial intelligence, energy dominance, health, space and agriculture.
"This is really an incredible collection of people that are working in service to the nation and really showcasing what the future of America is, where we're headed," said Gebbia.
President Donald Trump said he likes Elon Musk "a lot" after the pair faced a rift over the One Big Beautiful Bill earlier this year. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Gebbia says Americans shouldn't have to accept that their interactions with the federal government are going to be negative or difficult to navigate.

"What if people didn't say that? What if people have had a different sentiment? It's entirely possible they can. It takes a president who cares about this, it takes an administration who wants to invest in it, and it takes the right talent to build it."
"President Trump has those three things."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Unearthed: El-Sayed called for repealing law that made sex without disclosing HIV status a felony
summary: Abdul El-Sayed once called Michigan's HIV criminalization law "hateful" and "discriminatory," a stance now under scrutiny in his Senate race.
story: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is pressed by a student at a town hall over Iran and his past comments on Ali Khamenei.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed once called for repealing a Michigan law that made it a felony for people who knew they had HIV to have sex without first informing their partner — a position he is standing by eight years later as he campaigns in one of the nation's most competitive Senate races

As he unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018, El-Sayed repeatedly took aim at the law. The law carried a prison sentence of up to four years for people who knew they were HIV-positive and engaged in sexual penetration without first informing their partner of their HIV status.

"You should not be criminalized for a disease. That is absolutely wrong. It’s hateful. It’s discriminatory, and we can, as a state, do better. You can count on me for that," El-Sayed said as he ran for governor.
MICHIGAN STUDENT CONFRONTS EL-SAYED OVER IRAN STANCE

US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan Abdul El-Sayed speaks with reporters during a Student Meet and Greet at the Michigan Theatre in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on August 26, 2026. (JEFF KOWALSKY / AFP via Getty Images)

Fast-forward eight years and El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and a former health director for Detroit-anchored Wayne County, is battling former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the midterm race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The showdown in Michigan is a must hold for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the Senate from the GOP.

As he ran for the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial nomination — a contest he lost to now-two-term Gov. Gretchen Whitmer — El-Sayed's campaign website stated, "Repeal HIV/AIDS criminalization laws and the exclusion of transgender Michiganders from state Medicaid."

When asked in 2018 if he supported the decriminalization of HIV through legislation that would create two levels of misdemeanors, El-Sayed said at the time, "One of the big things that we have to recognize about HIV is that no disease can be illegal. The continuing forward of these laws on the books stigmatize people with the disease."
SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Michigan Democratic gubernatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigns at a rally on the campus of Wayne State University July 28, 2018, in Detroit, Michigan. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)

Whitmer also supported changing the law, which dated to 1988, saying as she ran for governor, "It’s wrong to criminalize sickness, which is what this law has effectively done. It absolutely should be revisited."

The law was reformed in early 2019, after passing a GOP-controlled legislature with broad bipartisan support. The revised statute limited the felony provisions to vaginal and anal intercourse involving an intent to transmit HIV or cases in which HIV was actually transmitted, reduced certain non-transmission offenses to misdemeanors and protected medically suppressed people from prosecution under the law's reckless-disregard provision.

"Abdul supports the bipartisan reform bill that passed in 2019 through a Republican legislature that eliminated the discriminatory laws on the books," campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital. "As a public health professional, Abdul has fought to support programs that stem the spread of diseases, including HIV."

Richner added that "the Trump administration has completely exacerbated this crisis by defunding the organizations and programs that do frontline care to prevent transmission and exposure in the first place. In the US Senate, Abdul will fight back against Donald Trump and RFK Jr’s attempts to dismantle our public health infrastructure and ensure all Americans have access to the care they need."
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Republican Senate nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers of Michigan stands for a Fox News Digital interview, on August 2, 2026, in Farmington Hills, Michigan (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
El-Sayed also stands by his past comments on fighting discrimination aimed at those with HIV.

Last week, as he landed an endorsement from the Human Rights Campaign, a leading LGBTQ advocacy group, El-Sayed highlighted that if elected to the Senate, "I’ll fight to ensure every Michigander can live without discrimination and never have to wonder whether their rights will still be there tomorrow."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

El-Sayed, who narrowly edged more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in August in a contentious primary that further exposed the rift between the party's left-wing and establishment factions, would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected.

He has made support for "Medicare for all" a major component of his campaign. El-Sayed has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and has been a vocal critic of Israel during its war against Hamas, characterizing Israel’s actions in Gaza as "genocide" against Palestinians.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Trump scores Supreme Court win in election integrity fight as states gain new voter roll tool
summary: An order issued Friday by the Supreme Court temporarily allows the Trump administration to move forward with a mass voter verification system.
story: Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley discusses the importance of voter verification after New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill revealed a software error led to 6,600 non-citizens being incorrectly registered to vote, with almost 400 casting ballots.
An order issued Friday by the Supreme Court temporarily allows the Trump administration to move forward with a mass voter verification system.

The emergency order allows states, for now, to use the Department of Homeland Security program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, in their efforts to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.

Because existing law blocks most states from systematically purging voters from their rolls within 90 days of an election, the immediate impact of Friday's order on the upcoming midterms is likely limited, the Associated Press reported. States' use of the SAVE program is voluntary.
Norm Eisen, a senior fellow with Brookings, agreed that the Supreme Court's ruling was restrained.

"Don't overreact to the SCOTUS SAVE database decision," Eisen wrote on X. "Page 6 of the decision makes clear that we are in the 90-day statutory window when mass changes can't be made to voter lists!"
LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES
An exterior view of the Supreme Court Building on June 22, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The court’s order puts on hold a federal judge’s June ruling that had deemed the Republican administration’s recently revamped version of SAVE illegal. U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan had blocked the use of the tool, saying it violated Americans’ privacy rights and could result in voters being wrongly removed from the rolls.
A federal appeals court declined to pause Sooknanan's ruling, prompting the administration's appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Trump administration moved to expand SAVE after the president signed an executive order directing the creation of a federal voter registration list and imposed new restrictions on eligibility for voting by mail as part of a broader effort to combat voter fraud.
TRUMP REVIVES SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION SHOWDOWN AFTER HOCHUL PARDON TORPEDOED FIRST CASE
Justices of the Supreme Court pose for their official photo at the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C. on Oct. 7, 2022. (Olivier Douliery/AFP via Getty Images)

The SAVE program was created in 1986 under an immigration law mandating that DHS help federal, state and local agencies prevent government benefits from going to noncitizens. The Trump administration last year moved to significantly expand its search abilities. Since then, at least 67 million registrations have been scanned through the program, but critics, the AP says, worry it could end up purging valid voters from the rolls.
Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor in dissenting.

President Donald Trump, left, and first lady Melania Trump walk to greet China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan as they arrive at the South Portico of the White House for tea, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington.  (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

"In my view… the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," Jackson wrote in a dissenting opinion. "This imbalance, along with the Government’s improbable merits arguments, should have compelled the Court to deny the stay."

But the majority pushed back on concerns that lawful voters could simply be removed from state voter rolls, noting that federal officials are required to contact individuals flagged by SAVE to seek additional information if their citizenship cannot be confirmed.

The majority also noted that SAVE has long allowed federal, state and local agencies to verify citizenship and immigration status using records maintained by the Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security and Department of State.

"The Supreme Court’s order allows the federal government to share information in its possession concerning people’s apparent citizenship status to help election officials register eligible voters while preventing the improper addition of non-citizens to the registration rolls," Michael Morley, director of the Election Law Center at Florida State University, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The Court recognized Congress expressly endorsed such information sharing in 1996 amendments to federal immigration law."

The Supreme Court's stay is temporary, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit could still rule against the SAVE program, potentially sending the case back to the Supreme Court.
Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said the Supreme Court already "got it right."

"The Trump Administration’s SAVE expansion just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls. Once again, left-wing interests are doing everything they can to block states from verifying citizenship on the eve of a federal election, and for the second time in a week they have lost in court. This a major win for election integrity."
Fox News' Shannon Bream, Bill Mears, Ashley J. DiMella and the Associated Press contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Flying sports car hides its wings as production gets closer
summary: Samson Sky's Switchblade flying car secures $80 million from Dubai's Matin Group, but the redesigned hybrid-electric aircraft still needs more testing.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have ever been stuck in traffic wishing your car could sprout wings, Samson Sky has been working on something pretty close. Its Switchblade flying car can drive out of your garage and take you to a nearby airport. Once there, the wings come out, the tail extends and the vehicle becomes an airplane. You heard right, an airplane. After landing, everything folds back inside so you can drive the rest of the way.

That idea has been around for years. What makes Switchblade worth another look right now is that Samson says it has secured an $80 million investment from Dubai-based Matin Group. Samson plans to use the funding to help move the project toward U.S. production. The company still needs another $20 million to fully fund its current production plan. That new backing gets the Switchblade closer. But what really caught my attention is how much Samson has changed since we first watched this flying car take off.
PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE
A rendering of the latest Switchblade design in flight mode, with its wings and tail fully extended. (Samson Sky)

Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward.
This flying sports car makes its wings disappear

The latest Switchblade design looks much more like a car when you are using it on the road. Samson says the wings, tail and propeller are now fully enclosed inside the vehicle during driving mode. That is a major change from the earlier design that completed its first flight in November 2023. When you reach an airport, the wings extend and the tail moves into position for flight. Samson says the transformation from driving mode to flying mode takes about three minutes.

After you land, the process reverses. The flight hardware folds back inside the body before you continue the trip by road. Samson says that setup allows the Switchblade to fit inside a standard garage while also protecting the flight surfaces when the vehicle is being driven or stored. There is still a runway involved, though. The Switchblade does not take off vertically from your driveway. You drive it to an airport, transform it into flight mode and take off from there.
The Switchblade we saw fly in 2023 has changed

We first covered the Switchblade after its official first flight on Nov. 5, 2023. The prototype flew from Grant County International Airport in Moses Lake, Washington. Since then, Samson has kept working on the version it hopes to put into customers' hands. The company has changed the design and increased the size of its engine. Samson says it plans to use three production prototypes for more testing around the end of 2026 or beginning of 2027.

So while we have already seen a Switchblade get off the ground, the version heading toward production has changed since that 2023 flight. That is why I am especially interested in what happens next. I want to see the latest Switchblade take to the air and show us what this new design can actually do.
How fast could the Switchblade flying car go?

Samson is targeting some attention-grabbing performance numbers. The company currently lists a maximum airspeed of 190 mph and a maximum flying range of 450 miles. It lists a maximum road speed of 100 mph. Samson also lists a 160 mph cruise speed. However, its FAQ says that anticipated figure still needs verification during production-prototype flight testing.

The Switchblade uses a hybrid-electric drivetrain. A gasoline engine powers a generator, which supplies electricity to the vehicle's motors. Samson says the system powers the wheels on the ground and the propellers in flight. The company currently lists a 44-gallon fuel capacity and says the vehicle uses 91-octane automotive gasoline.
HELMET-STYLE COCKPIT VISION SYSTEM AIMS TO CHANGE HOW PILOTS SEE IN LOW VISIBILITY
An earlier Switchblade prototype takes flight during the vehicle’s successful first flight in November 2023. (Samson Sky)
$80 million gives the Switchblade production push some muscle

Making a flying prototype and building vehicles for customers are two very different challenges. Samson says the new $80 million investment will help establish its first 180,000-square-foot Switchblade production facility in the U.S. The company signed a Joint Investment Agreement with Matin Group, and the two companies have started setting up a joint venture. Where that factory ends up remains an open question.

Samson Sky CEO and founder Sam Bousfield tells CyberGuy that the search has narrowed considerably, saying, "We will maintain our Samson Sky R&D Facility in Prineville, OR, and we have narrowed down the US production facility to three potential locations in different parts of the country, with some negotiations already begun." Samson has not identified those locations publicly. There is serious new money behind the production effort, but another financial hurdle remains. Samson says $20 million still needs to be raised before its current production plan is fully funded.
When could you actually get one?

Samson's current timeline points to summer 2027. The company says it expects its Builder Assist assembly line to be ready by then. Its first year of production will focus mostly on customers who previously paid for some of the earliest delivery positions. Depositors and reservation holders would follow. Then there is the price. Samson currently estimates the Switchblade VFR kit will start at $200,000. The IFR version carries an estimated price of $235,000. Those prices can still change before customer production gets underway.

Bousfield tells CyberGuy that reaching this point has been part of the plan for years. "It's been great developing the technology for a flying car that you park in your garage and is high performance in both modes. Now we get to put it out for people to use and explore the world around them." Before that happens, buyers will have to do something you probably have never done when purchasing a car.
Yes, you have to help build your Switchblade

Buying a Switchblade comes with homework. Samson plans for the aircraft to operate under the Experimental Amateur-Built category in the U.S. FAA rules require the "major portion," meaning more than 50%, of an eligible amateur-built aircraft's fabrication and assembly to be completed by people building it for their own education or recreation. That requirement is often called the 51% rule.

Samson says its Builder Assist program will guide owners through their portion of the process. The company says much of its manufacturing process will be automated and computer-driven. It estimates an owner can finish the required work in as little as one week. One regulatory detail deserves some attention here. The FAA says it evaluates aircraft kits to determine whether they can allow a builder to meet the major-portion requirement. The FAA does not approve or certify the kit itself. The finished aircraft also goes through the FAA airworthiness process. So this will be a very different experience from walking into a dealership, signing a few forms and driving home.
You will need to know how to fly it too

A Switchblade may drive like a vehicle on the ground, but once those wings come out, aviation rules take over. Samson says you will need a private pilot certificate to fly one. Ground licensing can vary based on where you register the vehicle. The company says an automobile or motorcycle license may apply depending on local regulations. That also separates Switchblade from some of the other flying vehicles we have been following.

Electric air taxis such as Joby's eVTOL are designed around vertical takeoff and landing. Switchblade takes another route. It uses conventional runways but gives you something an air taxi cannot: the same vehicle stays with you after you land. That could be useful on a regional trip. Instead of landing and then finding a rental car or arranging another ride, you fold the wings away and keep going.
WISCONSIN MAN FLIES HELICOPTER TO CABELA'S BECAUSE THE DRIVE WAS TOO LONG
A rendering of the Switchblade in driving mode, with its wings, tail and propeller enclosed inside the body. (Samson Sky)
What this means to you

Here's what makes the Switchblade so interesting to me. You could pull out of your garage, drive to an airport, fly hundreds of miles and then keep driving after you land. No rental car. No waiting around for another ride. The same vehicle goes with you from start to finish. The new funding gets Samson closer to making that happen, but I would not start clearing space in the garage yet. The company still has to finish funding its production plans, choose where to build the Switchblade and put the latest version through more testing. We have seen an earlier prototype fly, but the redesigned vehicle heading toward production still needs to show what it can do in the air.

And if you are thinking, "Where do I sign up?" there is a lot more involved than the estimated $200,000 starting price. You will need pilot training and access to an airport. You also have to take part in the Builder Assist process. For me, the next big moment comes when this latest Switchblade leaves the runway. If it can deliver on the speed, range and transformation Samson is targeting, this flying sports car suddenly gets a whole lot more interesting.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about the Switchblade is that the idea makes sense the minute you see how it works. You drive to the airport, fly to another city, fold the wings away after you land and keep going. The latest design makes that even more interesting because all that flight hardware disappears inside a vehicle you can park in your garage.

Of course, most of us are not shopping for a $200,000 flying sports car. The price alone puts the Switchblade out of reach for the majority of us, and becoming a pilot adds another wrinkle. But that does not mean you have to be a potential buyer to find this fascinating. I certainly am not planning to put one in my garage tomorrow, but I want to see whether Samson can actually pull this off.

The new funding gives Samson a much stronger push toward production, and we have already seen an earlier Switchblade fly. Now I want to see this redesigned version get into the air. If Samson can deliver what it is promising, we could be watching a pretty remarkable idea make the jump from a prototype we have followed for years to a flying sports car people can actually own.

Would you trust one vehicle to take you down the highway and into the sky, or would you want to see a few years of customer flights before climbing aboard? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Hacker claims 7.49M customer records stolen from American utility company
summary: CenterPoint Energy confirmed customer data was stolen, while a hacker claims 7.49 million records with partial Social Security numbers were taken.
story: Federal agencies issue an updated warning targeting municipal water and wastewater systems following cyberattacks in at least seven states. Chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on allegations of Iranian-affiliated hackers targeting critical infrastructure.

If you pay an electric or gas bill every month, you probably think about the amount due, not all the personal information sitting behind that account. But your utility company may have your home address, phone number, billing history and other details that can become very useful in the wrong hands. That is what makes the breach at CenterPoint Energy worth paying attention to, even if you have never been one of its customers.

CenterPoint says an unauthorized third party obtained personal information belonging to some customers through an external-facing system. A hacker, meanwhile, claims to have stolen 7.49 million customer records, including addresses, account numbers, billing information and partial Social Security numbers.

There is an important catch. CenterPoint has confirmed that customer information was stolen, but it has not confirmed the hacker's 7.49 million figure or the specific information the attacker says was taken. So, there are still plenty of questions about how big this breach really is. Here's what CenterPoint has confirmed, what the hacker is claiming and what you should watch for now.

DMV BREACH CONFIRMED AS HACKERS CLAIM 200,000 RECORDS STOLEN
CenterPoint Energy is investigating a cybersecurity incident that exposed personal information belonging to some customers. (CenterPoint Energy)
CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was stolen

CenterPoint Energy disclosed the incident in a Sept. 14 filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The Houston-based utility says it became aware of an online post from a third party claiming to possess a data set containing CenterPoint customer information.

CenterPoint then activated its cybersecurity incident response procedures and brought in outside cybersecurity experts. As the investigation progressed, the company determined that an unauthorized third party had obtained personal information belonging to some customers through one of its external-facing systems.

CenterPoint has not publicly said how many customers were affected. It also has not detailed which types of personal information were taken. The company says it plans to notify affected customers and regulators as required once it determines the scope of the incident.

CyberGuy reached out to CenterPoint Energy asking whether it could confirm the hacker's claim that 7.49 million records were stolen, what customer information was affected and whether a public API was involved. CenterPoint referred us to its SEC filing and provided this statement: "Our filing speaks for itself." The company did not provide additional details in response to our questions.

There is one piece of reassuring news for anyone who depends on CenterPoint for power or gas. The company says its electric and natural gas services continued operating normally during the incident. CenterPoint also says it currently does not expect the breach to have a material impact on its financial condition.
Hacker claims 7.49 million CenterPoint records were stolen
The bigger number comes from the attacker. A threat actor using the alias "4d722e4d656f77" told BleepingComputer that they obtained 7.49 million CenterPoint customer records.
According to the hacker, those records contain:
NamesPhone numbersService and billing addressesCenterPoint account numbersBilling amountsPartial Social Security numbers
Names
Phone numbers
Service and billing addresses
CenterPoint account numbers
Billing amounts
Partial Social Security numbers

The attacker later leaked the data after claiming CenterPoint ignored their attempts to make contact. Again, CenterPoint has confirmed that customer information was stolen, but it has not independently confirmed this list of exposed data or the 7.49 million record count. Also, 7.49 million records does not necessarily mean 7.49 million individual people were affected. One person or household can potentially appear in more than one record. CenterPoint says it is still working to determine the actual scope.
Hacker says a public CenterPoint system allowed automated data access

The attacker's explanation of how the theft allegedly happened may be one of the most interesting parts of this breach. The hacker told BleepingComputer they accessed the information by repeatedly cycling through millions of IDs using a public CenterPoint API.

An API allows different software systems to exchange information. Companies use them constantly behind websites and apps. According to the attacker, CenterPoint's API lacked protections that could have slowed or blocked mass automated requests. The hacker specifically claimed there was no effective rate limiting or web application firewall protection against the activity. CenterPoint's SEC filing does not confirm that attack method.

What CenterPoint does confirm is that the unauthorized third party obtained information through an external-facing system. That means we should treat the API explanation as the attacker's account until the company or investigators provide more technical details.
CenterPoint says an unauthorized third party obtained customer personal information through one of the company’s external-facing systems. (Annette Riedl/picture alliance via Getty Images)
FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS
Why stolen utility records can be valuable to scammers
A utility account may not seem as sensitive as a bank account. Yet it can hold exactly the kind of information a scammer wants before contacting you.

Think about how convincing this could sound: Someone calls and knows your name. They know your service address. They may know your CenterPoint account number or recent billing amount. Then they tell you there is a problem with your payment. That conversation can feel much more legitimate because the scammer already has information you would expect only the utility company to know.

Criminals can also combine information from one breach with details leaked somewhere else. A partial Social Security number, phone number or address may become more useful when paired with another stolen database. That is one reason I tell people to think about breaches as pieces of a much larger identity puzzle.

Stolen information can stick around for years. Criminals can save it, trade it and revisit it long after the original breach disappears from the news. You can read more about why last year's data breach can become this year's identity fraud.
Watch for fake CenterPoint calls, texts and emails

The immediate threat may not come from someone opening an account in your name. It could arrive as a text message. Once news of a breach becomes public, scammers can take advantage of the confusion even if they never obtained the stolen database themselves.

You could receive a message claiming CenterPoint needs you to "verify" your account after the breach. Another scammer might warn that your electricity will be disconnected unless you make an immediate payment. Be especially suspicious if someone creates urgency and then asks you to click a link, provide account information or move money.

If you receive a suspicious CenterPoint message, go directly to the company's official website or use the contact information printed on your bill. Avoid calling a number supplied in an unexpected message.
8 ways to protect yourself after the CenterPoint Energy breach
Whether you are a CenterPoint customer or simply wondering what you would do after your own utility provider suffered a breach, these steps can reduce your exposure.

CenterPoint says it intends to notify affected customers as required. If you receive a notice, read it carefully. Look for exactly what information CenterPoint says was involved and whether the company offers credit monitoring or other assistance. Do not rely on a text message or social media post claiming you were affected.

If CenterPoint’s breach notice confirms that Social Security information was involved, consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. It is free, and you can temporarily lift it when you legitimately need a lender to access your credit file. Keep in mind that a freeze cannot stop every kind of identity theft. Existing account takeovers and other fraud can happen without a new credit check.

Review your credit reports for accounts or inquiries you do not recognize. Then keep an eye on your bank accounts and credit cards for unfamiliar transactions. If something looks suspicious, contact the financial institution using the number on its official website, statement or the back of your card.

Your primary email account deserves extra attention because criminals can use it to reset passwords for other services. Use a strong, unique password and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Do the same for your utility account if the provider offers those protections. A password manager can create unique passwords so one stolen login does not give an attacker access to several accounts.
WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES
CenterPoint Energy says its electric and natural gas services remained operational and undisrupted during the cybersecurity incident. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

A scammer may claim you owe money and threaten to disconnect your electricity or gas immediately. Do not let the urgency rush you into paying. Hang up and contact the utility yourself through its official website or the customer service number printed on your bill.

A convincing breach-related email can still lead to a malicious website or malware download. Strong antivirus software can help detect phishing sites, malicious links and malware before they cause more trouble. Data brokers and people-search sites may already publish your phone number, address and other personal information. Removing that data will not erase information stolen in a breach. However, reducing publicly available information gives scammers fewer pieces they can use to build a detailed profile around leaked data. You can remove information manually or use a data removal service to handle recurring opt-out requests. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Identity theft protection can monitor credit activity and alert you when certain personal information appears in places where it could signal trouble. These services cannot prevent every form of identity theft. However, alerts can help you spot suspicious activity earlier. If you discover that someone has actually used your identity, document what happened and begin the recovery process quickly. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

A utility account can reveal more about you than you might expect. Your address, billing details and account information can give scammers enough personal context to make a fake call, text or email sound legitimate. We still do not know the full scope of this breach. That uncertainty is another reason to stay alert rather than wait for every answer before taking precautions. Watch your accounts, consider freezing your credit if sensitive information was exposed and be skeptical of urgent utility messages. We often have little choice about who provides our power or gas, which makes protecting the information customers hand over especially important.

If a company provides an essential service you cannot realistically live without, should it face tougher requirements for protecting the personal information you have no choice but to give it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Is everyone bricking their phone to stop doomscrolling?
summary: The $59 Brick device promises to help curb phone addiction, but free iPhone and Android tools may already do the job. Here's what to try first.
story: On 'Fox & Friends,' host Ainsley Earhardt talks with 'The CyberGuy' Kurt Knutsson, Phone Free New York founder Raj Goyle, and students Ana and Sara Goyle about the growing trend of school cellphone bans and their impact on student well-being.

There is a funny twist to the anti-FOMO craze. Now people are worried they may be missing out on the latest way to spend less time on their phones. You may have heard people talking about "bricking" their phones. Thankfully, they are not destroying them. A $59 product called Brick is getting attention because it lets you temporarily block distracting apps and websites, creating a physical barrier between you and whatever keeps sucking you back into your screen. I understand the appeal. If you have ever picked up your phone to check one text and resurfaced 40 minutes later wondering why you were watching a stranger remodel a bathroom, you know how quickly a quick check can turn into a scroll.

Still, my first reaction is this: before you buy another piece of technology to keep you away from technology, use the controls already sitting inside the phone you paid for. Apple has expanded Screen Time in iOS 27. Android already has some useful Digital Wellbeing controls. A few simple changes can also make distracting apps a little harder to reach and help break that automatic urge to grab your phone.
