CAN TECH REALLY GET YOU OFF YOUR PHONE AND INTO REAL LIFE?
A quick phone check can easily turn into a much longer scroll than you intended. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
More than half of Americans think they spend too much time on their phones

This trend is tapping into something much bigger than one gadget. Pew Research Center surveyed 9,750 U.S. adults from May 26 through June 1, 2026. It found 53% say they spend too much time on their smartphone. Among adults ages 18 to 29, that jumps to 70%. It stands at 64% among adults ages 30 to 49, then drops to 49% among people 50 to 64 and 25% among those 65 and older. Here is another number that grabbed me: 26% of U.S. adults say they use their smartphone almost constantly. Among adults under 30, that rises to 42%. A third of adults ages 30 to 49 say the same. Think about that phrase for a second. Almost constantly. Phones help us navigate, communicate and get an incredible amount done. I certainly would not want to give mine up. The problem begins when useful turns into automatic and you find yourself opening the same app without even remembering why you picked up the phone.
Plenty of people are trying to cut back

Awareness is already turning into action. Pew found 45% of U.S. adults tried to cut back on smartphone use during the previous 12 months. Among adults under 50, the figure reaches 58%. Yet among people who tried cutting back, only a quarter said they were extremely or very successful. That gap tells you a lot. Knowing you want to use your phone less and actually putting it down are two different things. The problem with willpower is that your phone is always right there, and the apps fighting for your attention are only a tap away. Teens are noticing the pull too. Pew found 45% of teens say they spend too much time on social media. Forty-four percent say they have cut back on social media use, and an identical share say they have cut back on smartphone use.
Your phone may also be stealing sleep

The effects can follow you right into bed. Pew found 62% of adults under 30 say their smartphone hurts the amount of sleep they get. Across U.S. adults overall, 41% say their phone hurts their sleep while only 5% say it helps. I suspect plenty of us know how that happens. The phone goes on the nightstand. You check one last thing, then another notification arrives. Before long, your bedtime has moved. That is why I think the bigger lesson in this trend is making distracting apps a little harder to reach. If opening an app takes more effort, you get a moment to decide whether you really want to go there.
TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS
The Brick helps cut down on screen time by physically locking access to distracting apps until you tap your phone to the device again. (Brick)
Why people are 'bricking' their phones

Brick takes that idea and turns it into something physical. First, you choose which apps or websites you want to block and create different modes inside the Brick app. To start a session, tap your phone against the physical Brick. Another option lets you begin remotely by pressing and holding the virtual Brick in the app for five seconds. Getting back into those blocked apps usually requires another tap against the physical Brick. That is the part I find interesting. Leave the Brick downstairs while you work upstairs, and your easy way back into those distracting apps is suddenly in another room.

The device currently costs $59 and supports iPhones running iOS 17 or later and Android devices running Android 12 or later. Head to CyberGuy.com to get 10% off the Brick with our link. One Brick can also work with multiple phones. Meanwhile, Strict Mode makes common workarounds harder, including deleting the Brick app or changing certain settings during a session. If you lose the device or cannot reach it, you get five Emergency Unbricks. I like the thinking behind it. Sometimes a physical barrier can work better than another warning on the same screen you are trying to stop staring at. Still, I would try the free controls already built into your phone before spending $59.
PHONE-FREE RESTAURANTS ARE TRENDING ACROSS THE US
Use Screen Time to put limits on distracting apps

Apple documents new Time Allowances and Screen Time Schedules in iOS 27. Apple also says all of your Apple devices need version 27 or later to use the latest Screen Time features across devices. If you do not see those newer options on your iPhone, App Limits and Downtime still give you useful ways to cut down on distracting apps.
Go to: Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit

Choose the app category you want to control. You can also tap a category to select a specific app instead. Tap Next, choose how much time you want to allow each day, then tap Done. For example, you could give yourself 30 minutes of Instagram or put a daily limit on your entire social networking category. It is a simple way to decide how much time you want to give an app before you are already deep into the scroll.
If certain times of day are your weak spot, Downtime can help.
Go to: Settings → Screen Time → Downtime → Scheduled

Choose Every Day or Customize Days, then set when you want Downtime to start and end. During Downtime, most apps and notifications are restricted, while phone calls and apps you choose to allow remain available. You can also turn on Block at Downtime if you want the limit to be harder to ignore.
OPINION: WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO
You can decide which apps stay available by going to: Settings → Screen Time → Always Allowed
That way, you can keep apps you genuinely need available without leaving every distracting app within easy reach.
Before setting any limits, spend a minute looking at where your time actually goes.
Go to: Settings → Screen Time → Daily Average

Tap Day or Week to see your usage. Scroll down to see Pickups and Notifications too. That pickup number may tell you even more than your total screen time. Maybe you spend only a few minutes at a time in an app but reach for your phone 80 times throughout the day. That tells me your challenge may be the habit of grabbing the device rather than one particular app. Start with whatever surprises you most.
Notifications can undo all your good intentions, and you do not need Apple Intelligence to quiet them.
Go to: Settings → Focus

Choose a Focus such as Do Not Disturb, Personal, Sleep or Work. From there, you can decide which people and apps are allowed to interrupt you. You can also add a schedule, so Focus turns on automatically during the parts of your day when you want fewer distractions.

This gets at something Screen Time alone cannot fix. Sometimes you did not decide to pick up the phone. The phone asked you to. Cutting down those invitations may be one of the easiest ways to stop checking it so often.
Checking your phone during work can break your focus and pull attention away from what you were trying to get done. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Android has free anti-doomscrolling tools too

Android phones include Digital Wellbeing tools that can show you how much time you spend in apps, how often you open them and how many notifications they send. Exact menu names can vary between Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones.
Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing
Tap the chart to see your screen time, how often you open apps and how many notifications you receive.
Set app timers
Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers
Next to the app you want to limit, tap Set timer , choose how much time you want to allow and tap OK . When your time runs out, the app closes and its icon dims. The timer resets at midnight.
Use Focus mode
Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Focus mode

Choose the apps you want to pause. While Focus mode is on, you cannot use those apps and their notifications stop. Tap Turn on now to start it immediately or Set a schedule to have it turn on automatically.
Set app timers
Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers

Tap Apps and app categories , then choose the apps or categories you want to control. Tap Add schedule , choose the days and amount of time you want to allow, then tap Save . Menu wording can vary slightly by Galaxy model and software version.
On current Pixel phones, you can also protect app limits with a separate PIN.
Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App limits → App limits PIN
Turn on PIN for app time limits , unlock your phone, then create and confirm a four-digit PIN. This adds another step before you can change a limit on impulse.
On Google Pixel
Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Bedtime mode → Bedtime routine

Choose when Bedtime mode should turn on. You can use a schedule or have it activate while your phone is charging during certain hours. You can also customize options including Grayscale, Keep the screen dark, Dim the wallpaper and Dark theme .
On Samsung Galaxy
Samsung handles this through Sleep mode .
Go to: Settings → Modes and Routines → Sleep

Tap When to start this mode, choose Sleep schedule , then set your usual sleep and wake times. Tap Save and then Done . You can also turn on options including Do not disturb, Grayscale and Dark mode while Sleep mode is active.
6 ways to win back attention from your phone
You do not need to overhaul your habits overnight. Start with your biggest distractions and make them a little harder to reach.

Check Screen Time on iPhone or Digital Wellbeing on Android. Look for the apps taking the biggest bite out of your day and how often you pick up or unlock your phone. Do not try to fix everything at once. Start with the biggest problem.
Every alert is another invitation to look at your screen. Keep the notifications that deserve immediate attention. Silence the ones that are simply trying to bring you back into an app.
Create your limits while you are thinking clearly instead of after you have already disappeared down a feed. Use App Limits and Downtime on iPhone or App timers and Focus mode on Android.

Move your worst offenders off the Home Screen. Log out when you finish. If you have to search for an app and sign back in, that gives you a little time to ask yourself whether you actually wanted to open it. You are creating your own speed bump.

Leave it somewhere else during dinner. Put it out of reach while you work. Charge it away from the bed. This may sound almost too simple, but sometimes distance works better than another setting buried inside a menu.

Try the free tools first. If you continually override every limit, delete every timer or find yourself reaching for the same apps anyway, then consider something stricter. That might be a stronger software blocker or a physical device such as Brick. By then, you will know exactly what problem you are paying to solve.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here is what gets me about this whole trend. We have reached a point where people are buying a piece of technology whose job is to keep them away from another piece of technology. That says something. I love what my phone can do. I do not want a dumb phone, and I certainly do not want to throw my smartphone in a drawer. What I want is to be the one deciding when I use it instead of reacting every time an app decides it wants me back. That is why I would start with what you already have. iPhone gives you App Limits, Downtime and Focus. Android gives you app timers and Focus mode. Your phone can also tell you exactly where your time went. Use that information. If those free controls work, you saved yourself $59. If you blow through every limit you create, Brick or another stronger blocker suddenly has a purpose beyond joining a wellness craze. For me, the real test is pretty simple: when you pick up your phone, did you decide to do it or did your phone decide for you?
If you could get back one hour of the time you spend on your phone every day, what would you do with it instead? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: The secret list that tells scammers you're an easy target
summary: Epsilon Data Management's "opportunity seeker" lists helped scammers target millions of older Americans, DOJ court filings reveal in detail.
story: ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner explains how his app helps protect older Americans from fraud and scams on ‘America’s Newsroom.’

Somewhere in a marketing database, something you did years ago could still be helping a company decide what you might respond to next. Maybe you entered a sweepstakes or signed up for a business seminar. That kind of response can become valuable data.

Federal court records show just how far that can go. In a case involving data broker Epsilon Data Management, employees had a name for people targeted by certain solicitations: "opportunity seekers." Those opportunity seeker lists became especially valuable when they reached people running fraud schemes. And as you'll see, the idea of sorting people based on what they are likely to respond to has not disappeared.

HOW SWEEPSTAKES ENTRY DATA CAN REACH SCAMMERS
Marketing data can reveal who has responded to certain offers before, giving scammers another clue about who may be more likely to engage. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What opportunity seeker lists actually mean

"Opportunity seeker" sounds like harmless marketing jargon. But in the Epsilon case, the Department of Justice (DOJ) showed how that label was being used inside a business unit that worked with fraudulent clients. According to Epsilon's deferred prosecution agreement, the company's clients included businesses sending deceptive solicitations involving sweepstakes, astrology, auto warranties, dietary supplements and government grants.

Epsilon employees called the people targeted by those offers "opportunity seekers" and referred to the clients sending them as "opportunistic." The court filing also says those opportunity seekers frequently came from the same group: older and vulnerable Americans.

Then there was the data behind the label. DOJ says Epsilon used transactional data and algorithms to identify "responsive buyers," or people most likely to respond to certain offers. Its database covered about 100 million U.S. households. Think about what that means. If you responded to one offer, that response could become a signal that you might respond to another. In the hands of a fraudster, that kind of information can make it much easier to decide who to target first.
This went far beyond one company

Epsilon eventually agreed to pay $150 million, including $22.5 million in criminal penalties and $127.5 million for victim compensation. Two former Epsilon employees, Robert Reger and David Lytle, were later convicted. A federal judge sentenced Reger to 10 years in prison and Lytle to four years.

According to the DOJ, they sold nearly 100 lists of names and addresses to one fraudulent client. That client used the information in a scheme that defrauded more than 218,000 people out of more than $23.7 million. Even more alarming, DOJ says more than 12,000 people were defrauded by that single scheme more than 20 times each.

Other cases followed. KBM Group entered a deferred prosecution agreement requiring a $33.5 million victim compensation payment and an $8.5 million criminal fine. DOJ says employees sold data tied to millions of Americans to more than a dozen clients they knew were engaged in fraudulent mass-mailing schemes.

Macromark, a Connecticut direct-mail services company, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud. The company admitted that lists it provided to fraudulent clients resulted in at least $9.5 million in losses. Wiland Inc. later entered a non-prosecution agreement with DOJ that included $4.4 million in victim compensation over data sold to operators of fraudulent schemes. By June 2025, DOJ said its Consumer Data Victim Compensation Fund had returned more than $129 million to more than 100,000 victims across the country.
A 2026 case shows this playbook is still alive

It would be easy to look at the earlier cases and think this was an old direct-mail problem. It wasn't. In May 2026, a federal judge sentenced Troy Murray of North Carolina to 121 months in prison after he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

DOJ says Murray collected and sold lists containing names, phone numbers, home addresses and, in some cases, ages and email addresses of older Americans. His customers included people in Jamaica running lottery fraud schemes. And the scale was huge. From 2016 through 2023, DOJ says Murray sent scammers at least 22,000 lead lists containing information on more than 7 million older Americans.

Those lists typically sold for $500 for 100 to 300 names. DOJ says Murray made more than $5.2 million while victims lost more than $9.5 million. That is what makes these lists so valuable to scammers. They do not have to spend time figuring out who might pick up the phone or respond to an offer. Someone has already handed them a list of people to try first.
WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE
Federal cases show how lead lists containing names, addresses, phone numbers and other personal details have been sold to fraudsters targeting older Americans. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The same kind of targeting is still sold as marketing

These kinds of marketing lists are legal and can be used for legitimate advertising. Just because a list is for sale does not mean the company selling it or the company buying it is doing anything wrong. But the way some of these lists are described today sounds very familiar.

As of September 2026, Geon Media advertises a list called "Prime Opportunity Seekers - Buyers Only!" It includes 397,532 names and focuses on people who purchased business opportunities after responding to marketing campaigns. Marketers can narrow that list even further using details such as age, income, net worth and location. Geon also requires buyers to provide a sample mail piece.

NextMark advertises a list called "Sweeps Winners Only" made up of people who recently responded to sweepstakes offers. Its listing describes that audience as "highly impulsive" and promotes the list for sweepstakes, lotteries, credit cards and other offers.

Exact Data also advertises categories with names including "Sweepstakes Opportunity Purchasers" and "Gambling, Lottery, and Sweepstakes Enthusiasts." Its listings were updated in September 2026. None of that proves fraud. What it does show is how valuable your past behavior can be. Respond to the right kind of offer, and that response can become a data point that helps someone decide what to put in front of you next.
Why your response history can be so valuable

For a scammer, finding someone willing to respond can be half the battle. Calling or emailing random people takes time. A list of people who have already responded to certain offers gives them a much better place to start. That is what made Epsilon's data so valuable. DOJ says the company's algorithms could predict which people were most likely to respond to certain mailings. If you had responded before, that behavior could become another clue about what might get your attention next.

And there is a lot of money on the line. The FBI says people over 60 filed more than 201,000 complaints in 2025 and reported more than $7.7 billion in losses. The FBI does not say how many of those people were targeted through marketing or lead lists, so we cannot say those lists caused those losses. But the DOJ cases show something important: scammers have used targeted lists to help find people they believe are more likely to respond. That is why something as simple as entering a sweepstakes or responding to an offer can be more valuable than you might think. The response itself can become another piece of data about you.
Even everyday actions like entering a sweepstakes or responding to a promotion can become another data point used to decide which offers you may see next. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
6 steps to make yourself harder to target

You probably cannot find every private marketing database that contains your name. However, you can reduce the information available about you and become much more selective about what you hand over going forward.

Start with your full name. Then search your phone number and home address. Pay attention to people-search sites displaying your address, age, relatives, phone numbers or email addresses. If you find a profile, look for the site's opt-out or removal process. The FTC says you can request removal from people-search sites yourself for free, although you may need to repeat the process if your information appears again later.

A legitimate contest can still collect information for marketing. Before entering, read the privacy policy and official rules. Look for language explaining whether your information can be shared with advertisers or marketing partners. The FTC specifically warns that contest promoters may sell information to advertisers, which can lead to more targeted advertising, promotional mail, calls and spam.

If an entry form asks for information that seems unrelated to the promotion, stop and ask why it needs it. Avoid handing over extra details simply because a box appears on a form. Also watch for prechecked boxes giving permission for additional marketing. Every unnecessary piece of information you share gives a company one more data point that can potentially be added to your profile.

Consider creating an email address or alias used only for contests, loyalty programs and promotional offers. That keeps your primary email address out of some marketing databases and makes unexpected prize messages easier to spot. If someone contacts your main email account claiming you won a contest you entered with a different address, that alone should raise questions.

This one is simple. Real prizes are free. The FTC says anyone demanding taxes, processing fees, shipping charges or other payments before releasing a prize is running a scam. Also, never provide your bank account, credit card or Social Security number to claim a prize. If you are unsure whether an offer is real, find the company's official contact information yourself rather than calling a number in the letter, text or email.

If you sent money or personal information to a scammer, act quickly. Contact your bank or payment provider first if money changed hands. Report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov . If the scam came through the mail, you can also report it to the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. If someone used your personal information, IdentityTheft.gov can walk you through recovery steps. For anyone age 60 or older, the DOJ's National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-FRAUD-11 (1-833-372-8311) offers free help Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern. DOJ says reporting certain financial losses quickly can improve the chances of recovering money, although recovery cannot be guaranteed.
What a personal data scan can and cannot tell you

There is no public search box that will show you every private marketing category attached to your name. A people-search or data-broker scan also cannot tell you whether your name appears on one of the specific "opportunity seeker" or criminal lead lists described above. And no data removal service can pull information back once criminals already have it.

What a scan can do is show you where personal details such as your name, address or phone number appear across covered people-search and data-broker sites. From there, you can start reducing that exposure. If the scan finds your information, you have two options. You can contact sites yourself and submit opt-out requests, or you can use a service that handles much of that work for you.

A data removal service can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of covered data brokers and people-search sites. Some plans also let you request removals from additional websites that fall outside the standard automated coverage.

It is worth knowing the limits too. Some private data-broker databases cannot be scanned directly. Instead, removal requests are sent to brokers that may hold your information. These services also cannot remove certain government records, court records or information already circulating in criminal databases.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

For me, the biggest takeaway here is that scammers do not always have to figure out who might respond. Sometimes, someone else has already done that work for them. The Epsilon case showed how marketing data and algorithms could identify people likely to respond to certain offers. DOJ says those "opportunity seekers" frequently included older and vulnerable Americans. And this problem has not been confined to old direct-mail cases. In 2026, a federal judge sentenced a man who DOJ says sold more than 22,000 lead lists containing information on over 7 million older Americans to lottery scammers. At the same time, legitimate marketers still sell highly specific lists based on things like sweepstakes responses and interest in business opportunities. That does not make those lists fraudulent. It does show just how much our past behavior can say about what we may respond to next. You may never know every list that has your name on it. But you can stop handing out unnecessary information, remove exposed personal data where possible and slow down whenever an unexpected offer lands in front of you.

Should companies be able to sell lists built around how likely someone is to respond to money-making or sweepstakes offers, especially when age and financial information can also be used for targeting? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Hackers hijack verified streaming account to spread malware, researchers find
summary: HBO Max's verified Reddit account was hijacked to push 108 malicious ads using ClickFix, a technique that tricks victims into running dangerous commands.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You probably know to be suspicious of a strange pop-up or a random website asking you to download something. But what happens when the ad comes from a verified account belonging to a company you recognize? That is what made a recent malware campaign involving HBO Max so concerning.

Researchers at Hudson Rock found that cybercriminals hijacked HBO Max's official, verified Reddit account and used it to push 108 distinct malicious ads over roughly 48 hours. The ads promoted HBO Max downloads along with AI tools, developer software and Mac utilities. Because they appeared under a verified corporate account, potential victims had one less reason to question what they were seeing.

You do not need HBO Max to be exposed to this type of attack. The larger lesson involves how criminals can borrow credibility from verified accounts and familiar companies to get people to lower their guard. And once you click, the attack can take a surprisingly simple turn.
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.
Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward.
SCAMMERS ARE BUYING GOOGLE ADS TO STEAL BANK LOGINS
Hackers hijacked HBO Max’s verified Reddit account to run more than 100 malicious ads, showing how trusted brands can be weaponized to spread malware. (Robert Way via Getty Images)
The HBO Max ad looked far more legitimate than a typical scam

The incident first surfaced after a Reddit user spotted an advertisement posted by the verified u/hbomax account. The ad promoted what appeared to be a native HBO Max application for macOS. HBO Max does not currently offer a native app for Mac computers. Its support page directs Mac users to stream at HBOMax.com. The user followed the advertisement to a convincing landing page. However, clicking the download button did not start a normal file download. Instead, the website displayed a prompt telling the visitor to copy and paste a command into Terminal. That request should immediately raise a red flag. Elsewhere in the broader PasteSwitch operation, Windows users could be routed through Run or PowerShell-based attack paths. Researchers found that the Windows branch could use PowerShell and other tools to eventually load malware directly into memory.
ClickFix tricks you into launching the malware yourself

The technique behind the campaign is known as ClickFix. Rather than relying entirely on a malicious download, ClickFix gives you instructions that lead you to execute the attack yourself. The prompt may pretend that something went wrong with a CAPTCHA. Another version may claim you need to fix a browser problem or complete an installation. A malicious webpage can even place a command onto your clipboard. Then it tells you where to paste it. That little sequence can feel like ordinary troubleshooting, especially when the page looks professional and the ad came from an account you trusted. In the HBO Max campaign, Hudson Rock says the technique relied on getting the victim to execute attacker-supplied code through Terminal. That approach can bypass some protections designed to stop malicious browser downloads. The warning sign I want you to remember is simple: A website should never need you to paste an unfamiliar command into Terminal, PowerShell or the Windows Run box to prove you are human or install ordinary consumer software.
The HBO Max account pushed 108 malicious ads

The fake HBO Max download was only part of what researchers uncovered. Hudson Rock says attackers used the compromised Reddit account to push 108 distinct advertisements during the roughly 48-hour campaign. The ads shifted between multiple software lures as domains were taken down or abandoned. The researchers counted:
40 ads tied to an HBO Max-themed domain36 ads promoting an AI and developer lure15 ads tied to a Mac system utility11 ads promoting another developer tool6 additional ads tied to an HBO Max Mac lure
40 ads tied to an HBO Max-themed domain
36 ads promoting an AI and developer lure
15 ads tied to a Mac system utility
11 ads promoting another developer tool
6 additional ads tied to an HBO Max Mac lure
That rapid switching shows how attackers can reuse the credibility of one compromised account while changing the websites and software names placed in front of victims.
Researchers connect the ads to a wider PasteSwitch operation

Hudson Rock and researchers from ADAMnetworks connected the HBO Max campaign to a broader operation they call PasteSwitch. The name describes what stays consistent across the operation: victims paste a command supplied by the attacker while the delivery system changes what comes next based on the visitor, platform and campaign.

That means two people clicking similar malicious ads may not necessarily receive the same malware. On Macs, researchers found several PasteSwitch payload paths. MacSync could steal browser credentials, Gecko browser profiles, Telegram data, Apple Notes and macOS passwords. Researchers also documented an AMOS helper chain that could maintain access to an infected device.

Another part of the operation used fake versions of cryptocurrency wallet apps, including Ledger, Trezor Suite and Exodus. Those fake apps were designed to steal 12- and 24-word cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases. That means one bad command could expose far more than the browser tab you were looking at.
CLICKLOCK MAC MALWARE LOCKS APPS UNTIL YOU GIVE IN
Cybercriminals used a verified HBO Max Reddit account to push ClickFix malware, tricking users into pasting malicious commands into Terminal or PowerShell. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Windows users faced a different malware path

PasteSwitch could also recognize Windows visitors and change its attack. Researchers found a Windows branch that used mshta and PowerShell. One route delivered a malicious file disguised in an MP3/HTA format before creating a scheduled task and launching PowerShell.

Later stages could inject the Amatera Stealer directly into memory without first writing the final malware to disk. Researchers also found a technique designed to make malicious traffic appear as though it were communicating with Facebook, potentially making basic network monitoring less useful. That level of technical complexity sits behind a remarkably simple first step: convincing someone to paste a command.
PasteSwitch can also tamper with crypto wallet addresses

Researchers connected PasteSwitch to another dangerous tool: cryptocurrency clipboard hijackers. The operation delivered malware known as AnimateClipper and ZigClipper. These tools can monitor the clipboard and replace cryptocurrency addresses when a victim copies or pastes them.

So, you might carefully copy the correct wallet address, paste it into a transaction and unknowingly send the money somewhere else. Researchers also found that the malware used Binance Smart Chain contracts to retrieve changing command-and-control domains. Between March and July 2026, researchers observed 36 changes made by the same attacker-controlled address. That helped the operation keep switching infrastructure as domains became unusable.
Why verified accounts and paid ads can fool careful people

Most of us make quick trust decisions online. A recognizable company name can make an ad feel safer. A verification badge adds credibility. When both appear together in a paid advertisement, the whole thing can look vetted. But verified accounts can still get compromised.

Hudson Rock says the attackers took advantage of HBO Max's trusted advertising identity during the campaign. The polished assets also helped lower the skepticism people might normally apply to an unknown online advertisement. That changes how we need to think about ads.

If an advertisement offers software you want, open a new browser tab and find the company's official website yourself. For apps, check your device's official app store. Those extra few seconds could stop the attack before it reaches your computer.
Reddit confirms the account was compromised

Reddit has now confirmed that an HBO Max account authorized to run advertisements on its platform was compromised and used to distribute malicious links. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, Reddit said:

"We recently learned that an HBO Max account authorized to run advertisements on Reddit was compromised and used to run ads containing malicious links. After learning of the issue, we locked the account, removed the ads and began working with HBO Max to strengthen its account security. At this time, we have not identified any impact to other Reddit advertising accounts."
We also reached out to HBO Max for comment but did not hear back before our deadline.
ClickFix has become a major malware delivery method

ClickFix has spread quickly because the attacker convinces the victim to take the final action. Huntress says ClickFix accounted for 53% of the malware loader activity it observed during 2025, based on its endpoint and identity telemetry. Attackers also keep changing the lure.

We have already seen fake CAPTCHA prompts spread through thousands of compromised websites and bogus Windows updates use similar techniques. Compromised websites can also display fake verification prompts designed to push visitors toward dangerous commands. The design may change next week. The request to run an unfamiliar command remains the behavior to watch for.
Your Mac may warn you, but do not depend on the alert

Apple has added another layer of protection against some ClickFix attacks. On macOS Tahoe 26.4 or later, Terminal may warn you when pasted text resembles a potentially harmful command. The warning explains that scammers sometimes persuade people to paste commands that can compromise their Mac or privacy. That protection can help, but users may not see a warning for every malicious command. Attackers also continue adjusting their techniques. Your own judgment still plays a major role.
'THE ODYSSEY' STREAMING SCAM COULD STEAL YOUR BANK INFO
Reddit confirmed the compromised HBO Max advertising account has been secured after malicious ads promoted fake downloads and malware. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
8 ways to protect yourself from malicious ads and ClickFix attacks
A convincing ad can get anyone's attention. These steps can help you recognize the warning signs before one bad click turns into a bigger problem.

A familiar logo or verification badge cannot guarantee that the person controlling the account today is the legitimate owner. When possible, visit the company's official website directly instead of clicking an ad.
If a webpage asks you to open Terminal, PowerShell or the Run dialog and paste something, close the page. Ordinary consumer software rarely requires you to run an unfamiliar command manually.
Use the developer's official website or your device's app store. Be especially careful when an advertisement suddenly offers a desktop application or special download you have never heard of.
Some ClickFix pages can copy malicious text onto your clipboard. If your browser or security software warns that a site copied something unexpectedly, take that warning seriously.
Security updates can add protections against newer attack techniques. Install updates through your operating system settings or the software's built-in updater.
Strong antivirus software can help block malicious websites and detect malware if an attack gets past your browser. It gives you another layer of protection when a convincing page slips through.

Disconnect the computer from the internet and run a full security scan using trusted antivirus software. From a clean device, change passwords for sensitive accounts, starting with your primary email account. Then review financial accounts and cryptocurrency wallets for activity you do not recognize.

An infostealer may capture passwords and browser information. Multifactor authentication can make stolen credentials harder to use, although some session-stealing malware can get around normal login protections.
Kurt's key takeaways

What caught my attention here was how quickly something dangerous could start to feel legitimate. The advertisement came from a verified corporate account. The page looked polished. Then the instructions presented themselves as a normal installation step. That combination can get past the skepticism many of us have learned to apply to obviously shady emails and suspicious websites. So I would focus less on how professional an advertisement looks and more on what it asks you to do next. The moment a website tells you to open Terminal, PowerShell or another system utility and paste an unfamiliar command, stop. Hackers will keep looking for ways to borrow the reputation of companies people already trust. We need to adjust our instincts as those attacks change.
Would you still trust an online ad because it came from a verified company account, or has this changed the way you decide what is safe to click? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: How the 'Squatter Hunter' is fighting home takeovers with tech
summary: Flash Shelton reveals how home security cameras and alarm systems can stop squatters before they claim tenant rights in your vacant property.
story: Flash Shelton, known as the "Squatter Hunter," recalls how he used everyday technology to get rid of squatters who had invaded his mother's property, in an interview with "The CyberGuy Report" podcast.

You leave a home empty while you travel, prepare it for sale or help an aging parent move. Then an unfamiliar car appears in the driveway. Someone gets inside. Before long, that person may even claim to have a lease. That kind of situation turned Flash Shelton into the man now known as the "Squatter Hunter." I recently sat down with Shelton on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to talk about how his unusual line of work began and what homeowners can do before an unwanted occupant settles in.

He stars in A&E's "Squatters," which follows him and his team as they help property owners reclaim homes from unauthorized occupants. What stood out during our conversation was how often his advice came back to technology. A camera alert or alarm can give you something that becomes much harder to get later: evidence of when someone showed up and how they got inside.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward.
HOMEOWNERS TERRORIZED BY PRO SQUATTERS TURNING DREAMS INTO NIGHTMARES IN PALM-LINED PARADISE, EXPERTS SAY
Flash Shelton helps property owners deal with unauthorized occupants and regain control of their homes. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson; JannHuizenga via Getty Images)
How protecting his mom created the 'Squatter Hunter'

Shelton says none of this started as a business idea. After his father died in 2019, he moved his mother in with him while preparing her vacant home for sale. Then seven people took over the property. Shelton told me he was "just being a good son" and felt he had to protect his mother after the squatters took advantage of the empty house. He called the sheriff and says he was told there was little law enforcement could do because the situation had become a civil issue. Shelton knew almost nothing about squatting at the time, but he did not accept that answer. "I was like, screw that. I'm going to do something about it," he recalled. He started researching how squatters operate and when occupancy claims can become harder to untangle.

His approach was unconventional. His mother, who owned the house, signed a legitimate lease giving Shelton the right to occupy the property. Shelton says he wanted documentation showing he had permission to be there in case the squatters produced a fake lease of their own. He then waited for the occupants to leave and entered the house using his key. Once inside, he started installing cameras and a security system. His thinking, he said, was that "if they can take a house, I can take a house." When some of the occupants returned, Shelton told them he had possession of the property and gave them until the end of the day to remove their furniture. He says cars and trucks soon arrived, and the house was cleared. Years later, that experience has turned into a full-time mission and an A&E series.
Why squatting is getting more attention across the US

Squatting can create a serious and expensive problem for homeowners, even though there is no reliable nationwide count showing exactly how often it happens. Part of the challenge is how these cases are tracked. Squatting does not appear as its own category in national crime databases, and cases can be handled differently depending on whether authorities view them as trespassing, fraud or a landlord-tenant dispute. That makes it difficult to put one national number on the problem.

What we do know is that lawmakers across the country have been responding. As of July 2026, the National Apartment Association reported that 28 states had enacted laws addressing squatting. Another 25 states have introduced or considered legislation during 2026. Those measures include faster removal procedures and new penalties for some forms of unauthorized occupancy. There are also documented cases showing how disruptive squatting can become. A New York City Department of Investigation review found unauthorized occupants in 548 vacant NYCHA apartments. Joint DOI and NYPD operations reclaimed 60 of those apartments and resulted in 81 arrests involving unauthorized occupants accused of criminal activity connected with the properties.

So while there is no single number showing how many homes are affected nationwide, the growing legislative response and documented cases make one thing clear: unauthorized home takeovers are a real problem, and homeowners have good reason to think about prevention before a property sits empty.
LAKE TAHOE SQUATTER SUSPECT CAUGHT ON SURVEILLANCE IN RICH-AND-FAMOUS MOUNTAIN RETREAT
No-trespassing signs can help establish that unauthorized visitors do not have permission to enter a property, though local rules vary. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The technology lesson Flash wishes he had learned sooner

For all the unusual tactics Shelton has used since becoming the "Squatter Hunter," his biggest piece of advice is surprisingly simple. Put cameras on a vacant property before there is a problem. Looking back at his mother's home, Shelton told me, "If I had cameras on my mom's house back then, I wouldn't be the squatter hunter today." The back door had been broken. What Shelton lacked was proof showing exactly when the entry happened and who did it.

He believes footage could have changed the situation from the beginning. With cameras, Shelton said, he could have shown authorities, "on this date, at this time, and this is the person." That is where today's home technology can make a real difference. A connected camera can alert you when somebody approaches a house. It can record an entry. It can also give law enforcement a timeline before competing stories about who belongs there begin.
Why a fake lease can complicate everything

One of the biggest challenges can appear after someone gets inside. Shelton says experienced squatters may produce a lease and claim they were given permission to live there. "They know that if they get into a property and show a lease and create reasonable doubt," Shelton told me, law enforcement may refer the property owner to the courts instead of immediately removing the occupant.

That is another reason camera footage can become so useful. A document may say one thing. Video showing someone forcing a door or entering a clearly vacant home can provide additional evidence about what actually happened. Shelton says many of the people he encounters understand how housing rules work and try to use tenant protections to delay removal.
Shelton says the goal is tenant rights, not adverse possession

You hear the phrase "squatters' rights" constantly, but it can blur together very different legal concepts. Adverse possession generally requires someone to occupy property openly for a period set by state law while meeting other specific requirements. That can take years. Shelton says the disputes he deals with tend to revolve around something much more immediate: whether an unauthorized occupant can create enough uncertainty to be treated as a tenant.

"Squatters are doing everything they can to gain tenant rights," Shelton told me. "They're not interested in squatter laws or rights. They want tenant rights." That helps explain why the legal response varies so much by state. Some states have created faster procedures for owners who say an unauthorized person took over a property. Others have increased penalties for fake leases or fraudulent documents.
ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS
Some cases go far beyond an empty vacation home

Shelton has dealt with situations that sound much more disturbing than somebody slipping into an abandoned property. During our interview, he described a case involving an 88-year-old woman in Culver City, California, who had hired a caregiver. According to Shelton, the caregiver lost the job but refused to leave the home. He said the situation eventually required intervention through social services and described it as a case involving elder abuse.

That experience sticks with him because the homeowner was especially vulnerable. Shelton has also worked on expensive properties. He recalled one Malibu home worth roughly $8 million and another case involving a Hollywood Hills mansion. His point was that there is no single profile of a property that can attract an unauthorized occupant. The same goes for the people involved. "They don't have a look," Shelton told me. "Squatters are your neighbors."
Shelton says squatters "don't have a look," so you may not be able to identify them easily. "Squatters are your neighbors," he said. (Fox News Digital/Kiera McDonald)
Be careful before trying the Squatter Hunter approach yourself

Watching Shelton confront people makes compelling television. Copying what you see on A&E could put you in a dangerous situation. The laws governing trespassing, tenancy and removal vary by state. If you discover somebody inside your property, call law enforcement and document what you can safely. Save camera footage. Preserve records showing when the property became vacant. Keep documentation identifying anyone who had permission to be there. If someone claims to be a tenant, an attorney familiar with local property law can help determine the appropriate next move.

Shelton brings years of experience into these encounters. He also has experience with de-escalation, which is another reminder that the confrontations you see on television come with risks. That is very different from a homeowner walking into a house alone and confronting a stranger.
Flash Shelton ultimately wants to put himself out of business

The growing attention around squatting has turned Shelton into a television personality and given him more cases than he can handle. But he says his long-term goal goes in the opposite direction. "There are no shortage of cases" where people need help, he told me. Still, Shelton said, "I ultimately want to change these laws and put myself out of business."

In the meantime, his biggest message for homeowners has less to do with dramatic confrontations. Pay attention early. A camera can tell you someone arrived. An alarm can tell you a door opened. A neighbor can tell you a moving truck has suddenly pulled into the driveway. Once somebody has spent time inside and starts claiming the right to be there, the situation can become much more complicated.
NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE'
Flash Shelton's tips to help protect your home from squatters

During our conversation, I kept asking Shelton the question most homeowners probably have: What can I actually do before this happens? His advice focuses on making a vacant property easier to monitor while reducing the signs that nobody is around.

Start with cameras covering the most likely entry points. Shelton likes the fact that systems today allow homeowners to check their property remotely. As he told me, "you can be anywhere in the world" and monitor what is happening at home from your phone. Look for motion alerts and person detection. Night vision can help when someone arrives after dark. Also check how your recordings are stored. If an incident occurs, save important clips so they do not disappear when a cloud-storage retention period expires. You can see my picks for the 12 best outdoor security cameras at CyberGuy.com.

A camera becomes a lot less useful if the electricity goes down. Shelton says he often works with battery-powered cameras because properties do not always have active power or internet access. Some batteries can keep a camera running for weeks or months, depending on the model and how frequently it records. He also recommends checking the backup capabilities of an alarm system. Before leaving a property vacant, Shelton told me to "make sure you've got cameras, your alarm system, everything's up-to-date." That means testing the system before you leave instead of assuming last year's setup still works. For a more complete setup, see my Best Home Security Systems 2026 guide at CyberGuy.com.

Shelton recommends timers for indoor lights and solar-powered security lighting when permanent power presents a problem. He also likes rechargeable lights with battery backup. That way, the house does not suddenly go completely dark during an outage. A smart plug or connected bulb can also let you adjust lighting remotely. The goal is to avoid broadcasting that a property has been sitting untouched.

One of Shelton's most practical tips costs nothing. Tell trusted neighbors when a house will be vacant and make it clear whether anybody has permission to enter. As Shelton put it, "Your neighbors, they don't want you to have a squatter either." Ask them to contact you if an unfamiliar vehicle repeatedly appears in the driveway or someone begins carrying furniture inside. Shelton relied on a neighbor himself at his mother's house. The property had no Wi-Fi, so a neighbor allowed him to use a nearby connection for his camera. That option will depend on range and the equipment involved, but the larger lesson still works. A neighbor can notice activity before you ever receive a call from anyone else.
During "The CyberGuy Report" interview, the "Squatter Hunter" explains how his mother’s vacant home takeover pushed him to start helping other property owners. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Shelton says people scouting vacant properties can pay attention to mailboxes. An overflowing box may signal that nobody has been around. He also worries about an unauthorized occupant receiving mail at an address and later presenting it as evidence that they live there. "Make sure you have a mailbox that is lockable," Shelton advised. If you are traveling, arrange to have your mail held or picked up. Also, pay attention if correspondence begins arriving for unfamiliar people at a property that should be empty. Our CyberGuy vacation guide has more on mail holds and home security before a trip: 6 things to do before you leave on vacation.

Putting up a no-trespassing sign sounds obvious. Shelton says homeowners should find out whether their local law enforcement agency offers an additional step. He told me that some sheriff's departments allow owners to file a form documenting that a property has been posted against trespassing. Why bother? A person can pull a sign down. Shelton described the thinking pretty simply: someone sees the notice, removes it and later says, "What sign?" Having something on file with local authorities may help document the owner's wishes even if the physical notice disappears. Procedures vary, so check directly with your local sheriff or police department before relying on this strategy.
SAN FRANCISCO HOME WITH HISTORY OF SQUATTERS UNDER CONTRACT FOR $1.3 MILLION

Shelton also recommends thinking about the clues people can see from the street. Put lights on timers. Keep the yard maintained. Avoid leaving packages outside. If practical, Shelton suggests leaving a vehicle in the driveway. He even recommends asking a trusted friend whether they can park there while you are away. None of that guarantees somebody will stay away. It can make a vacant property less obvious to a person scouting for an easy target.

If you plan to be gone for a week or longer, Shelton recommends doing one final security check before you leave. "Make sure you've got cameras, your alarm system, everything's up-to-date," he told me. Check camera batteries. Make sure motion alerts reach your phone. Confirm that your alarm is communicating properly. Also think about what happens if someone cuts the power or the neighborhood has an outage. Shelton recommends equipment with battery backup whenever possible. A few minutes spent testing everything before you leave could prevent you from discovering later that the camera you were counting on stopped recording days earlier.

A squatter moving into a property does not automatically gain legal ownership of it. However, homeowners should also be aware of a separate threat called home title fraud. Criminals can use fraudulent documents or stolen personal information to try to change property records or obtain financing tied to a home.

That makes property-record monitoring another layer of protection. A home title monitoring service can alert you to certain changes involving your property records, including a new owner, new lender or changes in financing. Home title monitoring cannot stop someone from entering your property or prevent a fraudulent filing. However, an alert can help you spot an unexpected change and investigate it sooner. See my tips and best picks on home title monitoring services at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

What happened at Flash Shelton's mother's house shows how quickly a vacant property can become somebody else's opportunity. For me, the most useful part of his story comes before any confrontation. Shelton wishes he had cameras running when people first entered his mother's home. That says a lot. The sooner you know somebody has entered your property, the sooner you can call for help and preserve evidence showing what happened. I also would not overlook the low-tech advice. Tell a trusted neighbor when a property should be empty. Pay attention to the mailbox. Find out what your local police or sheriff recommends before you need them. And remember that the law is changing quickly. With 28 states now having enacted measures addressing squatting, you should check the rules where your property is located rather than assuming something you saw online applies everywhere. You can hear my full conversation with Flash Shelton on The CyberGuy Report podcast.
Should states make it easier for homeowners to remove squatters quickly, or could tougher laws go too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI robot may stop your dog from barking while you're gone
summary: WIM-Z's AI dog training robot uses on-device processing to detect barking and dispense treats autonomously, with field trials showing up to 83% reduction.
story: Wonderdog chief medical officer Dr. Evan Antin joins 'Fox & Friends' to explain their new AI health companion for dogs. The platform tracks over 40 different analytes from regular at-home blood draws, detecting illnesses like kidney degradation before symptoms manifest. This proactive approach aims to prolong pets' lives and help owners understand their dog's long-term health.

If your dog starts barking the second you walk out the door, leaving home can come with a little extra guilt. That can happen whether you live in an apartment or a house. A pet camera can show you what is happening, but watching from your phone does little when your dog reacts to every sound outside or gets anxious when you are gone.

WIM-Z wants to take a more active role. The small tracked robot uses on-device artificial intelligence to watch your dog and respond to certain behaviors. Once the robot is in position, it can identify your dog, detect barking and decide when to reward calmer behavior with a treat. You can also speak through the robot and drive it around your home from your phone.
AI ROBOT FOR SENIORS CAN ALERT FAMILY AFTER A CALL FOR HELP
WIM-Z is designed to move around the home with your dog, using AI to detect barking and reward calmer behavior with treats. (WIM-Z)
Now WIM-Z has shared early field results, and its first customer units will make behavior and training decisions on their own while owners control where the robot moves.
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com
How the WIM-Z AI dog training robot works

WIM-Z stands for Watchful Intelligent Mobile Zen. The robot measures about 11 inches tall and rides on rubber tank-style treads. Its camera turret can pan 270 degrees and tilt more than 120 degrees. A side cartridge holds up to 44 treats.
Inside, WIM-Z uses a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8 AI accelerator. The company says its onboard AI can identify individual dogs, classify barking and track a dog with its pan-and-tilt camera.
Once WIM-Z detects barking, its behavior system can decide whether to intervene without waiting for you. The robot can then use a calming cue and dispense a treat when appropriate.

However, there is an important limit. WIM-Z does not currently drive itself around your home looking for your dog. You control that movement through the app, or you can leave the robot in one location.
WIM-Z also includes two-way audio. Its app can show behavior activity and optional highlight clips, giving you another way to see what happened while you were away.
WIM-Z says barking dropped by as much as 83%

WIM-Z recently released results from seven field trials conducted between May and September 2026. Six took place in homes around the New York metro area. One took place at a kennel in Jersey City. Across the trials, four hand-built robots logged 50 sessions and about 60 hours of use. WIM-Z says the system detected more than 2,100 barks. It also made 107 autonomous interventions and dispensed about 500 rewards.

The biggest numbers came from two homes that ran repeat autonomous sessions over two to three weeks. In one home, barking fell from 161 barks per hour to 40, a 75% reduction. In the other, barking fell from 317 barks per hour to 53, an 83% reduction. WIM-Z also reported that more interventions ended with the dogs going quiet as the trials progressed.
ROBOT DOG COULD DELIVER YOUR NEXT PACKAGE AND AN AD
The WIM-Z robot combines a movable camera, two-way audio and a built-in treat dispenser in its tracked design. (WIM-Z)
Why the reward-based approach stands out

WIM-Z takes a gentler approach. Instead of using shocks, sprays or scolding, it relies on treats and calm cues to reinforce better behavior. That lines up with guidance from the American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior, which recommends reward-based training and warns against aversive methods.

The bigger question is whether the AI can read the situation well enough to respond appropriately. A dog barking at a delivery person is very different from one that is distressed because you left. WIM-Z has to recognize that difference and react at the right moment for the approach to work well.
What WIM-Z can and cannot do on its own

WIM-Z can handle the behavior side on its own. Its onboard AI can identify a dog, track it with the pan-and-tilt camera, detect barking, decide when to intervene and dispense a reward without you making each decision. What it cannot do yet is navigate your home on its own. You drive WIM-Z from room to room through the app, or you can leave it in one spot where your dog spends time.

The first customer units will work this way, combining autonomous behavior and training features with owner-controlled movement. Full self-navigation, where the robot maps your home and goes looking for your dog by itself, remains on the company's roadmap and will not be included in the first units. So, WIM-Z can decide how to respond to your dog, but you still decide where the robot goes.
What happens to your video and data?

Any mobile robot with a camera and microphone deserves a privacy check before you let it roam around your living room. We asked WIM-Z exactly what happens to the information it collects. The company says all AI processing happens on the robot itself. That includes behavior detection, bark classification and decisions about when to intervene. No video is sent to the cloud for AI analysis.

Some information can still leave the robot. Event data such as bark activity, behavior interventions, treat dispensing and battery status are stored on an Amazon Web Services relay server so it can appear in the app's activity history. If you connect remotely, live video and two-way audio stream through WIM-Z's relay using encrypted WebRTC technology. The company says these are live streams to your phone, not recordings, and they are not stored on its servers.

Optional highlight clips work differently. Short selected clips can be uploaded for assembly and playback in the app, but WIM-Z says continuous footage is never uploaded. Owners can delete clips at any time or turn the feature off completely. The company says those clips are deleted within 90 days after an account is deleted.

WIM-Z also told CyberGuy that it does not sell customer data. Customer footage is not used to train its AI models unless the owner explicitly opts in. When the robot is used only on local Wi-Fi without remote access, the company says nothing leaves the home.

We have raised similar questions with other connected home robots because a camera that can move around your house gets access to very private spaces. Those answers give us a much clearer idea of how WIM-Z handles your information. Still, I would review the privacy controls before bringing any connected camera into my home.
ONE-WHEELED AI SECURITY ROBOT COULD PATROL YOUR PROPERTY
WIM-Z uses its camera and on-device AI to monitor a dog’s behavior and respond with calming cues and rewards. (WIM-Z)
How much WIM-Z costs and when you can get one

WIM-Z will cost $799 for the first production units. Right now, the company is taking a fully refundable $99 deposit to hold a spot. WIM-Z told CyberGuy it expects the first batch to ship from late Q4 2026 through Q1 2027. That means the first units could arrive between the end of 2026 and early 2027.

The company also acknowledges that hardware schedules can slip. If WIM-Z has not shipped your unit by Q2 2027, it says your deposit will be refunded automatically. WIM-Z says the deposits are held through Stripe and are not placed in the company's operating account.

The company says it has built five robots so far. Four are still being used in the field, while another is in Shenzhen, China, for production evaluation with a manufacturer. That gives you a pretty good sense of where things stand. WIM-Z is still in the early stages, so reserving one now means you are getting in before the product has been widely released and used in homes.
What this means to you

If your dog tends to bark or get restless when you leave, WIM-Z shows where pet tech may be headed next. Instead of simply alerting you that something is happening, the robot can respond while you are away by using a calming cue and rewarding your dog when it settles down.

There is one thing to remember with the first version. WIM-Z will not roam around your house looking for your dog by itself. You will need to position it where your dog spends time or drive it remotely through the app.

Still, I would not count on a robot to solve serious separation anxiety. The ASPCA says dogs with moderate or severe separation anxiety may need gradual behavior work with an experienced professional. For barking or mild restlessness, though, a robot that recognizes what your dog is doing and responds at the right time could be a useful extra set of eyes at home.

The early results are interesting, but I want to see what happens when WIM-Z is tested with many more dogs in different homes. I also want to see how well the first production units perform once customers start using them. For now, WIM-Z has an interesting idea, some encouraging early numbers and a much clearer picture of what buyers will actually get.
Kurt's key takeaways

WIM-Z caught my attention because it tackles a problem pet cameras mostly leave in your hands. Seeing your dog bark from miles away can make you feel helpless. WIM-Z's onboard AI can make a training decision and reward calm behavior without waiting for you to step in. I also like that the first version keeps movement in your hands. You control where the robot goes, while the behavior and training system can operate on its own. Full self-navigation may come later. Keeping the AI processing on the robot means your video does not need to go to the cloud for behavior analysis. Remote features and optional highlight clips can still send some information outside your home, so you will want to understand those settings. At $799, I would still want to see more testing and hear from real customers once the first production units start shipping. But if WIM-Z can build on these early results, it could become a useful tool for dog owners who worry about what happens after they walk out the door.
